sections.html:
Bartlesville is in Washington County, in northeastern Oklahoma, and a small piece of the city reaches into Osage County. The Caney River divides downtown from the east side. The 2020 census counted 37,290 residents and 17,140 housing units, with 11.7 percent vacant. Owners lived in 66.3 percent of occupied homes and renters in 33.7 percent, so investors and landlords are regular buyers next to owner-occupants.

The city is about 21 square miles and mostly built out. Incorporated in 1897 and platted in 1898, it has older neighborhoods around downtown where houses are close to a century old. Original plumbing, wiring and foundations in those homes get close attention from a buyer's inspector.

Almost all of the Washington County part of town is in Bartlesville Public Schools, Independent School District 30. A few northern areas fall in Dewey, and some Osage County sections are covered by Dewey and Osage Hills. US-75 runs north and south, US-60 east and west, and State Highway 123 also serves the city. Buyers who commute to Tulsa, about 45 miles south, often ask about drive time.

Two floods and a tornado come up in buyer questions. The Caney River flooded in October 1986 after unusually heavy rain and split the city in half for several days. It broke its banks again in June 2007 and crested five feet below the 1986 level. An EF4 tornado struck Bartlesville and nearby Barnsdall on May 6, 2024, so buyers often ask whether storm repairs were permitted and finished.

The city warns that some properties lie in floodplains or floodways. Development there can be regulated or prohibited, and a floodplain development permit may be required before you add to or alter a structure. If your house is near the river, expect a buyer to ask about flood zone status and insurance. Check your parcel with the city's engineering department before you list.

The Building and Construction Services division handles permits. Call 918.338.4244 before any project to find out whether a permit applies. Unpermitted work is a common source of delay at closing, so check before you list or accept an offer.

WorkPermit needed?
Structural construction, alteration, demolition, remodel, re-roofing that changes the roof structureYes
Fences over seven feet, walls over four feetYes
Electrical, including solar and generatorsYes
Furnaces, water heaters, fuel-gas pipingYes
Plumbing (faucet repairs and clearing stoppages are exceptions)Yes
Pools or hot tubs 24 inches or deeperYes
Painting, tile, carpet, cabinets, like-for-like doors and windowsNo

The city enforces the state's minimum construction codes, adopted by the Oklahoma Uniform Building Code Commission.

The Neighborhood Services Division enforces minimum property maintenance codes and usually acts on complaints rather than patrolling. Common violations are tall grass and weeds, junk and trash, deteriorated fences and structures, broken windows, parking on grass, inoperable vehicles, improperly stored recreational vehicles and illegal signs.

More than 2,000 complaints are filed and investigated in a year, and about 97 percent end in voluntary compliance. File one online, at City Hall, 401 S. Johnstone Ave., or by phone at 918.338.4230. Call the same number to learn whether anything is open on your address.

Owners of vacant or run-down buildings can look at the Voluntary Demolition Program, which allows demolition of dilapidated structures at a reduced fee and avoids nuisance actions. Participation is voluntary and funding is limited. A neglected inherited house with open complaints is a common reason owners here look at a direct sale.

sections.h2: How property tax works in Washington County
sections.html:
The Washington County Assessor values every property as of January 1, and the county treasurer bills the tax. Each property is visually inspected at least once during a four-year revaluation cycle. The assessor sets value, not the tax rate. Schools, cities and townships set levies after public hearings.

Disagree with a value? Start with an informal protest by visiting the assessor, who arranges a follow-up inspection. You can then file a written protest with the county Board of Equalization, an independent three-member board. If that fails, you may appeal to district court within twenty days after the Board adjourns or twenty days after May 31, whichever is later.

Reach the assessor at (918) 337-2830 and the treasurer at 918-337-2810. Homestead status matters at sale time: report it if you sell or stop living in the house as your primary residence.

Tax you still owe typically comes out of your sale proceeds. Ahead of listing, phone the treasurer for today's balance, and ask the assessor what happens to your homestead filing once you sell.

  1. Get a written balance from the treasurer at 918-337-2810.
  2. Ask Neighborhood Services about open code complaints.
  3. Check permits for past work, especially roofs, plumbing and electrical.
  4. Check flood zone status if the house is near the Caney River.
  5. Collect your roof, furnace and storm repair records.

Open items and put-off repairs make a lender-financed sale harder, since inspectors and appraisers write them up. A cash buyer will usually look at the house as it stands and price the repairs in.

Bartlesville grew up around oil, and energy employers still anchor the job market, so many sellers here are relocating for work on short notice. If a transfer date is driving your timeline, tell the buyer early. A cash sale can close around a moving date in a way a financed sale with an appraisal and repair negotiation often cannot.

A deed in Oklahoma carries a documentary stamp tax of 75 cents per $500 of the price. The Washington County Clerk collects it at recording. Anyone who makes, signs, issues or sells the deed can be on the hook, and the grantee can be held responsible as well, so settle in your contract who pays. In practice that is a line item on the settlement statement.

Separately, a seller of one or two residential units hands the buyer one of two forms under 60 O.S. section 833: a property condition disclosure or a disclaimer. Pick the disclosure and you will be describing the roof, plumbing, electrical and other systems, so answer carefully and accurately.

Summers are hot, winters cool and spring is the wet season, with severe weather most likely April through June. The swing from triple digits in summer to deep cold in winter is hard on roofs, HVAC equipment and exposed plumbing. Any buyer will price in stained ceilings, a patched roof or an aging furnace, and cash buyers run the same arithmetic.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house in Bartlesville with code violations?
faqs.a: Yes. Open complaints will not block a sale, though you should resolve or disclose them. Buyers discount for them. Neighborhood Services at 918.338.4230 can tell you what is open.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to repair a roof in Bartlesville?
faqs.a: It depends on the work. Re-roofing that changes the roof structure or framework needs a building permit, and the division suggests calling 918.338.4244 to confirm before you start.

faqs.q: Who do I call about my Washington County valuation?
faqs.a: Call the county assessor at (918) 337-2830. Values are set as of January 1, and an informal protest comes first, then the Board of Equalization, then district court.

faqs.q: Is Bartlesville in a flood zone?
faqs.a: Parts of it are. The Caney River flooded the city in 1986 and 2007, and some properties lie in floodplains or floodways. Check your parcel with the city's engineering department before you list.

faqs.q: What documentary stamp tax applies to a Bartlesville sale?
faqs.a: The rate is 75 cents per $500 of consideration, paid when the deed is recorded with the county clerk. Your contract says who pays.
